content: Vesicular and bullous lesions should be evaluated systematically to ensure that serious underlying causes are not overlooked. The initial step involves determining whether the lesions are localized or diffuse. A detailed history of the lesions should be obtained, including their onset, progression, and associated symptoms. A thorough review of systems and a focused physical examination are essential components of the evaluation. If the etiology of the lesions is not immediately apparent, referral to a dermatologist is recommended. Differential Diagnosis Localized Lesions: Allergic Contact Dermatitis: This condition arises from a hypersensitivity reaction to an allergen that comes into direct contact with the skin. Bullous Impetigo: A bacterial skin infection, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, characterized by superficial blisters that rupture easily. Insect Bites: Lesions caused by bites from various insects, which may present as vesicles or bullae depending on the reaction. Burns: Thermal or chemical burns can result in blister formation due to damage to the epidermis. Diabetic Bullae: Patients with diabetes may develop spontaneous, non-inflammatory bullae, typically on the lower extremities. Dyshidrotic Eczema (Pompholyx): A chronic, relapsing condition characterized by small, deep-seated vesicles on the palms, soles, or sides of the fingers. Friction Blisters: These occur due to repetitive mechanical trauma, often seen on areas of the skin subjected to friction. Herpes Zoster (Shingles): A reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus, presenting as a painful, unilateral vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV): HSV infections can cause grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, often recurring in the same location. Diffuse Lesions: Blistering Diseases: These include autoimmune conditions such as bullous pemphigoid and pemphigus vulgaris, which are characterized by widespread blister formation. Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT): A disorder of heme metabolism that leads to photosensitivity and blistering on sun-exposed areas. Polymorphous Light Eruption: A photodermatosis presenting as pruritic vesicles, papules, or plaques following sun exposure. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN): Severe mucocutaneous reactions, often triggered by medications, characterized by widespread epidermal detachment and blistering. Varicella (Chickenpox): A viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus, presenting as diffuse vesicular lesions in various stages of evolution. Additional Considerations: A skin biopsy should be performed if conditions such as PCT, pemphigus, or bullous pemphigoid are suspected to confirm the diagnosis. Laboratory testing, such as obtaining a culture for HSV-2, should be conducted if herpes simplex virus infection is suspected.
